_purpose: ✒️ Executive Enactment Record — the formal actions, curated from primary sources. Wave 1 (Phase 3) seeded five actions; wave 2 added EO 14156 as its own row and backfilled EO 14151's standing history. This file is the single source of truth for the lane's action data: netlify/database/migrations/20260807000000_seed_exec_actions_wave1.sql and 20260808000000_seed_exec_actions_wave2.sql write the same rows into the vr_* spine, and exec-action-data.js is generated from this file by scripts/gen-exec-action-data.mjs. scripts/test-exec-seed.mjs asserts they all agree, so the SQL and the client data cannot drift apart.
_readBy: scripts/gen-exec-action-data.mjs (generates exec-action-data.js — regenerate after every edit)
_shape: Exactly the shape actionsFor() / standingOf() in exec-record.js already read: actionClass, documentId, title, actedAt, term, sourceUrl, sourceLabel, issues[{issueKey, direction, isPrimary, weight, rationale}], status[{status, effectiveAt, authority, sourceLabel, sourceUrl, basis, note}]. Nothing here is a new vocabulary — every actionClass is a key of db/exec-action-types.json#actionClasses, every direction is a key of #issueDirections, every status is a token of db/exec-summary-keys.json#buckets.actions, and every issueKey is in db/issue-keys.json.

_sourcingRules.sourceOfRecord: Per db/exec-action-types.json: congress.gov for signed legislation, federalregister.gov for orders. whitehouse.gov appears nowhere in this file, not even as a secondary link — every action here had a primary citation available, so no secondary was needed.
_sourcingRules.standingCitation: Every status entry carries its own source_url and source_label, and a `basis` naming what kind of document establishes it. An action with no citable standing gets NO status entry rather than an assumed one; exec-record.js routes it to unstatedStanding and discloses it as 'with no confirmed standing on file'.

basisValues.enacted_law_published: The standing is established by the enrolled text as published by GPO — the law exists and nothing in the file repeals it. Claims enactment and publication; claims nothing about litigation.
basisValues.court_ruling: The standing is established by a ruling this pass read in full from the court's own opinion. The strongest basis, and the only one that can support 'blocked', 'partly blocked' or 'struck down'.
basisValues.register_disposition: The standing is established by the Federal Register document record, whose disposition notes are the authoritative register of revocation and supersession BY LATER PRESIDENTIAL ACTION. Deliberately narrower than court_ruling: it says the order stands as published and unrevoked, and says nothing about any challenge to it. Every entry using this basis states that limit in its note.
basisValues.register_continuation: Wave 2. The standing is established by a Federal Register notice continuing a time-limited authority — specifically a National Emergencies Act declaration, which expires one year after it is declared unless the President continues it (50 U.S.C. 1622(d)). Separated from register_disposition because it answers a different question: not 'has this been revoked' but 'has this lapsed'. It carries the same limit — a continuation is a presidential act and says nothing about any challenge to the order.
basisValues.pending_litigation: Wave 2, and the ONLY basis that may support challenged_unverified. The row is established by a primary court filing showing a live challenge — a complaint or docket document read in this pass — and by the absence of any ruling resolving it in the same docket. It is strictly weaker than court_ruling and can never support blocked, partly blocked or struck down: a complaint is an allegation, and this basis reports that the allegation is on file and unresolved, not that it is correct. Every entry using this basis names the case, the court, and what the docket did and did not contain when it was read.

_whyNoScore: There is no score field anywhere in this file and no count that could become one. See exec-record.js's header: the set of orders a president could have signed is unbounded and self-chosen, so any ratio computed over these rows would divide by a number we picked.

_verificationPass.method: Every citation below was fetched and read in this pass, not carried over from curated text. Federal Register facts come from the FR API document records (title, signing date, publication date, FR citation, document number, disposition notes). Public Law facts come from GPO's published PLAW packages. Standing facts come from the courts' own opinions and orders, downloaded as PDF and read — the operative disposition, not a summary of it.
_verificationPass.refused: congress.gov returns HTTP 403 to this environment, as it has to every prior voting-record pass (see 20260804000000's header). The congress.gov bill pages below are cited as the source of record because db/exec-action-types.json names them as such and the repo's whole congressional lane already cites them; the FACTS asserted about those two laws were verified against GPO instead, which does answer.

wave2.added: EO 14156 (own row, three status rows), EO 14151 (three appended status rows), and the challenged_unverified standing token.
wave2.courtSources: courtlistener.com's HTML site also returns HTTP 403 to this environment and its docket-entries API requires credentials, so dockets were read through the unauthenticated search API (type=r, fielded queries) and every document was then downloaded in full from storage.courtlistener.com and read as text. Rate limited to 5 requests a minute, which is why the docket sweeps in these notes are narrow and named rather than exhaustive.
wave2.negativeFindings: Two claims here rest on the ABSENCE of a document, which is the weakest kind of finding and is therefore stated as what was searched rather than as fact: (1) the W.D. Wash. docket for EO 14156 was queried for injunction / dismissal / order entries and returned only pro hac vice orders, and the docket is not terminated — hence challenged_unverified rather than a ruling token; (2) the FR disposition record for EO 14156 contains no revocation entry. Neither is a guarantee that nothing exists; both are a statement of what this pass looked for and found.

_circularityRule.why: WHY SOME MAPPINGS CARRY circularWithStance. PDXWordAction's third rule is that a position is never its own test. word-action.js#isIndependentWord already catches the blatant form of the violation — a card that leads with a record verb AND cites the clerk or congress.gov. What it cannot catch is a card that asserts a view in the figure's own voice and then cites the very document that would test it, which is the NORMAL shape of a presidential stance card: these cards were largely written FROM this record. Left alone, feeding these actions into the consistency engine would have produced a dense, near-total agreement read that measured nothing except the fact that a card and its own source agree.
_circularityRule.howItIsApplied: The flag sits on an action→issue PAIR, not on an action and not on an issue. That is the whole point: a stance stays testable by a DIFFERENT document. energy_production is flagged against Executive Order 14154 and Executive Order 14156, whose titles its card quotes, and is scored against Public Law 119-21, which its card does not mention. consistency.js pairs this declared flag with a mechanical identifier match over the card's own text and evidence (order number, public-law number, measure number, exact title) and suppresses scoring when EITHER signal fires, so a later card rewrite that starts naming a document is caught without anyone remembering to edit this file.
_circularityRule.whatAFlagDoesNotDo: A flagged pair still ships and still counts as coverage — it is real, sourced record, and the lane renders it. It simply cannot be scored. The reader sees the action and the position side by side and is told the position was written from that action, which is more honest than either hiding the action or counting it as a match.
_circularityRule.whyNotJustDeleteThoseMappings: Because the mapping is true. Public Law 119-1 really does advance deportations; the flag records why that true mapping cannot serve as evidence about this particular figure's consistency, which is a different claim. Deleting it would lose real record to protect a score.

trump.title: Laken Riley Act
trump._citationNote: S. 5, not H.R. 29, is the vehicle that became Public Law 119-1. The two bills shared the name; the House-numbered one never left the Senate calendar. The repo already had this wrong once and repaired it in 20260804000000 — this seed attaches to the corrected identity, and GPO's PLAW-119publ1 enrolled text carries '[S. 5]' on its face.

issues.rationale: Mandates detention and removal proceedings for covered unauthorized immigrants.
issues.circularNote: The stance card on this issue names this law as its own evidence — it reads "signing his first law — the Laken Riley Act (Public Law 119-1)" and cites the bill page as its source. A card written from this document cannot also be the word this document tests.

issues.rationale: Tightens immigration enforcement.
Triggered by arrest for burglary, theft, larceny, shoplifting, assault of a law enforcement officer, or any crime resulting in death or serious bodily injury.
Gives state attorneys general standing to sue the federal government over certain immigration-detention and enforcement decisions.

trump._issuesNote: Not re-authored here. These are the four vr_measure_issues rows S. 5 already carries, read straight across with supportMeaning yea_supports rendered as direction 'advances'. The EER and the 🏛️ lane therefore cannot disagree about what this law does.

status.authority: Passed by Congress and signed by the President
status.sourceLabel: GovInfo — Public Law 119-1, enrolled text as published by GPO
status.note: Enacted and published as Public Law 119-1, approved January 29, 2025. Nothing on file repeals or amends it. This states that the law exists and stands as published; it is not a statement about any challenge to it.

trump.title: To provide for reconciliation pursuant to title II of H. Con. Res. 14
trump._titleNote: The official title, taken from GPO's PLAW-119publ21. The enacted law carries NO act-wide short title: 'One Big Beautiful Bill Act' does not appear as the name of the Act in the enrolled text, only as a section-level short title deep inside it. The app's congressional-lane data calls the measure by the popular name, which is how readers will search for it, so this row keeps the official title and the popular name is left where it already is rather than being propagated into a second lane. Flagged in the Phase 3 notes; not changed here, because renaming a measure the 🏛️ lane renders is not a seed's business.

issues.rationale: Extends and makes permanent the 2017 individual income-tax rates.
Makes the 2017 individual income-tax rates permanent and adds temporary deductions for tips and overtime pay.
Reduces federal spending across several mandatory programs.
Nonpartisan CBO analysis projects the Act adds trillions of dollars to federal deficits over ten years.
issues.circularNote: The stance card on this issue is titled "H.R.1: Deficit & Debt" and exists to report this law's projected deficit effect. The card is downstream of this document, so this document cannot test it.

issues.rationale: Offsets part of its cost with Medicaid and SNAP reductions the CBO estimates leave millions more people uninsured.
issues.circularNote: The stance card on this issue is titled "H.R.1: Medicaid & SNAP" and exists to report this law's projected coverage effect. The card is downstream of this document, so this document cannot test it.

issues.rationale: Funds border-barrier construction and border enforcement personnel.
Phases out and repeals clean-energy and electric-vehicle tax credits enacted in 2022.
Appropriates tens of billions of dollars for immigration detention and removal operations.
Raises the child tax credit to $2,200 per child and makes it permanent.
Expands onshore and offshore oil, gas, and coal leasing and speeds fossil-fuel permitting.
Adds a large increase in defense and military spending.
Opens additional federal lands and waters to energy leasing.
Restricts graduate and parent student-loan borrowing and repayment options.
Creates a federal tax credit for donations to K-12 private-school scholarship organizations.

trump._issuesNote: THE OMNIBUS SPLIT, and the reason this lane is not a scoreboard. Fourteen issue mappings, four of them 'opposes' — read across from the vr_measure_issues rows H.R. 1 already carries (five from db/vr-issue-seed.json, nine from 20260720000000_hr1_omnibus_component_issues.sql), with supportMeaning yea_supports/yea_opposes rendered as advances/opposes. One signature therefore reports in both directions, exactly as one roll call on H.R. 1 does in the 🏛️ lane. Curating only the headline issue would have let a signed omnibus look like a single clean win.

status.authority: Passed by Congress and signed by the President
status.sourceLabel: GovInfo — Public Law 119-21, enrolled text as published by GPO
status.note: Enacted and published as Public Law 119-21, approved July 4, 2025. Nothing on file repeals it. This states that the law exists and stands as published; it is not a statement about any challenge to it.

trump.title: Unleashing American Energy
trump._dedupeNote: ONE energy action, not two. The app's curated spotlight data carried this order twice for Trump under one headline that also folded in a second, separate order — 'Declared a national energy emergency to expand production' described BOTH 'Unleashing American Energy' and 'Declaring a National Energy Emergency' (EO 14156, 90 FR 8433, doc 2025-02003, signed the same day). Two documents inside one card cannot be given a standing each, which is precisely what the Standing axis needs. This seed carries EO 14154 alone; EO 14156 arrived in wave 2 as its own row below, with its own citation and its own standing — and the two standings are now different, which is the evidence that splitting them was not pedantry.

issues.rationale: Directs agencies to expedite oil, gas and mineral permitting and leasing and to remove regulatory barriers to domestic energy production.
issues.circularNote: The stance card on this issue cites this order by title — "Signed the 'Unleashing American Energy' and 'National Energy Emergency' executive orders". The issue is tested instead by Public Law 119-21, which that card does not name.

issues.rationale: Revokes the previous administration's climate executive orders. The Federal Register disposition record for this document lists the revocations by number, including EO 13990 and EO 14008.

trump._issuesNote: The 'opposes' mapping is not an inference about intent — it is read off the Federal Register's own disposition notes for this document, which enumerate the orders it revokes. That is why a sole-authored order can also report in both directions.

status.sourceLabel: Federal Register — Executive Order 14154 document record, 90 FR 8353
status.note: Published at 90 FR 8353 and not revoked or superseded by any later presidential action in the Federal Register's disposition record for this document. That is the whole of the claim: it describes the order's status in the register, NOT the outcome of any challenge to it. This pass found no ruling enjoining EO 14154 itself; the litigation it appears in concerns agency implementation of funding provisions, and the appellate ruling there (4th Cir. No. 25-1575, decided 2026-01-21) vacated the district court's injunctions rather than extending them.

trump.title: Declaring a National Energy Emergency
trump._splitNote: The other half of the folded card described in EO 14154's _dedupeNote above, now standing on its own. Signed the same day as EO 14154 and about the same subject, and still a different document: a different FR citation (90 FR 8433, pp. 8433–8437, doc 2025-02003), a different legal mechanism (a National Emergencies Act declaration that unlocks emergency permitting authorities, rather than a set of policy directives), and — the point of the split — a different standing. EO 14154 stands unchallenged in this file; this one is in active litigation. Folded together, one card would have had to pick one of those two answers and would have been wrong about the other document.

issues.rationale: Declares a national energy emergency and directs agencies to use emergency authorities to expedite domestic energy production, transportation, refining and generation.
issues.circularNote: The stance card on this issue cites this order by title and opens by narrating it — "Declared a national energy emergency at the start of his second term". The issue is tested instead by Public Law 119-21, which that card does not name.

issues.rationale: Sections 4 and 5 direct emergency Clean Water Act and Rivers and Harbors Act permitting by the Army Corps of Engineers and emergency Endangered Species Act consultation procedures for energy projects on federal land and water.

Section 8(a) defines the 'energy' the emergency covers as crude oil, natural gas, lease condensates, natural gas liquids, refined petroleum products, uranium, coal, biofuels, geothermal heat, the kinetic movement of flowing water and critical minerals — wind and solar are absent from the definition, so the emergency's expedited procedures are unavailable to them.

trump._issuesNote: The 'opposes' mapping on climate_action is read off the order's own text, not inferred from its subject: Section 8(a) is an enumerated definition, and what it leaves out is as operative as what it includes, because the emergency authorities in Sections 3 through 6 reach only the listed resources. Weighted below the primary mapping because the order does not repeal any climate measure — it routes around them for one set of resources.

status.sourceLabel: Federal Register — Executive Order 14156 document record, 90 FR 8433
status.note: Published at 90 FR 8433 and carrying no revocation in the Federal Register's disposition record for this document. That is the whole of the claim: it describes the order's status in the register, NOT the outcome of any challenge to it. The later rows in this log are what report the challenge.

status.sourceLabel: Federal Register — Continuation of the National Emergency With Respect to Energy, 91 FR 1667 (doc 2026-00732), signed Jan. 12, 2026
status.note: A National Emergencies Act declaration expires after one year unless it is continued, so this row exists to answer a question the first row cannot: the order did not lapse on January 20, 2026. The notice states 'I am continuing for 1 year the national emergency declared in Executive Order 14156', under 50 U.S.C. 1622(d). CITATION CORRECTION: the Federal Register's own disposition note for EO 14156 cites this as 'Notice of January 12, 2026 (91 FR 1661)', but 91 FR 1661 is a different document (doc 2026-00698, a Foreign Assistance Act delegation). The continuation is doc 2026-00732 at 91 FR 1667, which is what this row cites and what was read. A continuation says nothing about any challenge to the order.

status.authority: Challenge pending — U.S. District Court for the Western District of Washington (State of Washington v. Trump, No. 2:25-cv-00869-JNW)
status.sourceLabel: W.D. Wash. — State of Washington v. Trump, No. 2:25-cv-00869-JNW, First Amended and Supplemental Complaint (ECF 55, filed Jan. 30, 2026)
status.note: THE CURRENT STANDING, and it is a statement about this file rather than about the order. Seventeen States are suing over this order; its paragraph 1 reads 'This case concerns an Executive Order issued on January 20, 2025, EO 14156, 90 Fed. Reg. 8433 (January 29, 2025)', and the prayer for relief asks the court to declare EO 14156 unlawful and to enjoin the agencies implementing it. The docket was filed May 9, 2025 and is not terminated; as read in this pass it carries no preliminary-injunction ruling and no ruling on the pending motion to dismiss. So no court has stopped this order and no court has upheld it — 'in force' would assert the second of those, which is why this row does not say it. Dated to the operative amended complaint, the document actually read, rather than to the docket's filing date.

trump._standingNote: Why the challenge row is last and not the continuation row: current standing is the latest row by effective_at, and a presidential continuation does not resolve a lawsuit. Had the continuation been filed after the challenge it would still have carried challenged_unverified, for the same reason — the President continuing his own emergency is not a court answering the question that is open.

trump.title: Ending Radical and Wasteful Government DEI Programs and Preferencing

issues.rationale: Directs the termination of federal diversity, equity and inclusion offices, positions, programs and related grants and contracts.
issues.circularNote: The stance card on this issue cites this order's own subject — "Signed executive orders ending federal DEI programs and preferencing" — and links the order itself. No other action on file reaches this issue, so it stands as coverage rather than as a test.

status.authority: U.S. Court of Appeals for the Fourth Circuit
status.sourceLabel: Fourth Circuit — National Association of Diversity Officers in Higher Education v. Trump, No. 25-1189 (published opinion, Feb. 6, 2026)
status.note: The facial challenge to this order reached judgment: the Fourth Circuit VACATED the district court's preliminary injunction and remanded for further proceedings, so no injunction against the order is in effect. Read from the court's own published opinion, which closes 'we vacate the district court's order granting plaintiffs' motion for a preliminary injunction, and remand for further proceedings. VACATED AND REMANDED'. The case continues on remand; a later ruling would arrive as a further row in this log rather than a change to this one.

status.authority: U.S. District Court for the District of Maryland (Judge Adam B. Abelson)
status.sourceLabel: D. Md. — National Association of Diversity Officers in Higher Education v. Trump, No. 1:25-cv-00333-ABA, Preliminary Injunction of Feb. 21, 2025 (ECF 45)
status.note: BACKFILL — the first standing this order held, appended behind the current one. 'The Motion is GRANTED IN PART and DENIED IN PART': the court preliminarily enjoined this order's Section 2(b)(i), the Termination Provision, in part — together with two provisions of a different order, EO 14173, which are not this row's subject. Partly blocked and not blocked: one provision of this order was enjoined and the rest was not, and the Enjoined Parties are 'Defendants other than the President' and those acting in concert with them, not the President himself. Read from the injunction order itself, not from the accompanying memorandum opinion (ECF 44).

status.authority: U.S. Court of Appeals for the Fourth Circuit
status.sourceLabel: Fourth Circuit — National Association of Diversity Officers in Higher Education v. Trump, No. 25-1189, Order of Mar. 14, 2025 granting a stay pending appeal (D. Md. ECF 73)
status.note: BACKFILL — 'we grant the government's motion for a stay of the preliminary injunction', entered at the direction of Chief Judge Diaz with the concurrence of Judges Harris and Rushing, applying the Nken v. Holder factors. The injunction stopped operating, so the order was operative again — which is why this row reads in force. A STAY IS NOT A MERITS RULING: the same order set an expedited briefing schedule and the appeal remained pending until the February 6, 2026 decision above, which is the row that resolved it. This row is what 'in force' is licensed to mean here and no more.
status._whyNotChallenged: This is the case the new challenged_unverified token was NOT used for, and the distinction matters. A primary ruling exists here and this pass read it, so the honest report is what that ruling did. challenged_unverified is for the state where no such ruling exists — see EO 14156 above. Using it here would file a read document as an unread one.

status.authority: U.S. District Court for the District of Maryland (Judge Adam B. Abelson)
status.sourceLabel: D. Md. — National Association of Diversity Officers in Higher Education v. Trump, No. 1:25-cv-00333-ABA, Order of June 30, 2026 dismissing the case (ECF 107)
status.note: THE CURRENT STANDING, found while verifying the docket for the backfill above and appended rather than folded into the earlier row. On remand the plaintiffs filed a notice of voluntary dismissal without prejudice and the court accepted it: 'it is hereby ORDERED that the notice is ACCEPTED. The Clerk is directed to CLOSE this case.' The case is closed and no injunction against this order is in effect. WITHOUT PREJUDICE and by the plaintiffs' own choice — no court held this order lawful, and this row does not say one did. It supersedes the February 6, 2026 row's closing sentence ('the case continues on remand'), which was true when written; the earlier row stays as filed because the log is append-only.

trump._standingBackfill: DONE in wave 2, additively. The two rows wave 1 held back — the District of Maryland's February 21, 2025 preliminary injunction and the Fourth Circuit's March 14, 2025 stay of it — are now on file above, each read from the court's own document and each carrying its own citation and basis. The February 6, 2026 row that was here first was not rewritten or moved; the whole point of an append-only log is that history can be filled in behind the current standing without disturbing what was already published. A fourth row, the June 30, 2026 dismissal, was found while verifying the docket for this backfill and appended in the same way. Array position is not meaning here: current standing is the latest row by effective_at, computed in exec-record.js's standingOf(), so these rows sit at the end of the array in the order they were appended while reading as history in the UI.

trump.title: Preserving and Protecting the Integrity of American Elections

issues.rationale: Section 2(a) directs the Election Assistance Commission to require documentary proof of United States citizenship on the federal voter-registration form.
issues.circularNote: The stance card on this issue cites this order by number: "Signed EO 14248, 'Preserving and Protecting the Integrity of American Elections'". No other action on file reaches this issue, so it stands as coverage rather than as a test.

issues.rationale: Directs federal agencies to share data to identify ineligible registrants and directs enforcement of ballot-receipt deadlines against States that count late-arriving ballots.

trump._axisBNote: THE WORKED EXAMPLE FOR THE WHOLE LANE, and the reason the standing log is append-only. Three rulings, three citations, one row each — a mutable status column would have kept only the last and lost the other two. Every entry stays 'partly blocked': parts of this order are permanently enjoined and other parts are not, and neither 'in force' nor 'blocked' would be a true one-word answer at any point in this sequence.

status.authority: U.S. District Court for the District of Columbia (Judge Colleen Kollar-Kotelly)
status.sourceLabel: D.D.C. — LULAC v. Executive Office of the President, Nos. 25-0946 / 25-0952 / 25-0955 (CKK), Memorandum Opinion of Apr. 24, 2025
status.note: Sections 2(a) and 2(d) PRELIMINARILY ENJOINED; the motions were DENIED as to Sections 2(b), 7(a) and 7(b), which were left free to operate. Read from the court's own opinion, whose disposition names each section separately.

status.authority: U.S. District Court for the District of Columbia (Judge Colleen Kollar-Kotelly)
status.sourceLabel: D.D.C. — LULAC v. Executive Office of the President, Nos. 25-0946 / 25-0952 / 25-0955 (CKK), Memorandum Opinion of Oct. 31, 2025
status.note: Escalation, not resolution: on partial summary judgment the court PERMANENTLY ENJOINED implementation of Section 2(a) and entered a final, appealable judgment on those separation-of-powers claims. Certain Administrative Procedure Act claims were dismissed without prejudice for want of final agency action. The rest of the order was not enjoined, so the standing stays 'partly blocked'.

status.authority: U.S. District Court for the District of Columbia (Judge Colleen Kollar-Kotelly)
status.sourceLabel: D.D.C. — LULAC v. Executive Office of the President, Nos. 25-0946 / 25-0952 / 25-0955 (CKK), Memorandum Opinion of Jan. 30, 2026
status.note: The current standing. The court DECLARED that Sections 2(d) and 3(d) cannot lawfully be implemented and PERMANENTLY ENJOINED them; dismissed the claims directed at Sections 4(a), 7(a) and 7(b) for want of standing or final agency action; and left claims touching Sections 2(b) and 3(a) for further proceedings, subject to strict Privacy Act compliance. Parts of the order are permanently enjoined and parts are still operative — which is what 'partly blocked' means, and why one word for the whole order would be false either way.
